opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that an RL environment is really just a structured way of saying "here's a task, here's how the model interacts with the world to do it, and here's how we decide whether it did a good job." And once you have that, it becomes this pretty portable artifact. You can point it at an open-weights model and actually do gradient updates, or you can point it at a closed model and use it more as an evaluation harness, or for things like prompt optimization, or as a way to generate and filter data.

With open models, the exciting part is that you can close the loop. You take a capable base, say a mid-sized open model, and you run RL against environments that look a lot like the actual work you care about: multi-turn tool use, coding in a real repo, navigating some internal API. What we've seen is that you can get surprisingly large gains on those narrow distributions without needing frontier-scale compute, because the model already has most of the latent capability. RL is mostly teaching it to reliably use what it already knows in your specific setting.

With closed models, you obviously can't touch the weights, unless the provider exposes some kind of reinforcement fine-tuning API, which some now do. But the environment is still really valuable. It tells you where the model fails, it lets you compare models honestly on your task rather than on some public benchmark that's been saturated, and it gives you a reward signal you can use for things like best-of-n sampling or optimizing the scaffold around the model.

So I don't really think of it as open versus closed. The environment is the durable thing. Models are going to keep changing, every few months there's a new one, but if you've invested in a really good environment with a really good reward signal, that keeps paying off no matter what model you're plugging in. And I think that's a big part of why there's been so much energy around building shared, open environment ecosystems, so people aren't each rebuilding the same harnesses from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response describes RL environments as portable task and evaluation artifacts, mentions gradient updates for open models, and lists data generation/filtering as one possible use. It does not frame them as engines for creating training data to optimize both open and closed models.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify distillation from one model into another as a use of examples created through an RL environment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that an environment is really just a specification of a task plus a way to grade it. You've got some setup, some way for the model to take actions or produce an output, and then a reward signal that tells you how well it did. And once you frame it that way, the question of open versus closed becomes a lot less about the model and a lot more about who controls the training loop.

With open models, the environment is the whole story. You can take something like a Qwen or a Llama checkpoint, build an environment around a task you actually care about, whether that's tool use, agentic coding, some domain-specific reasoning thing, and run GRPO or whatever your preferred algorithm is directly against it. You see the gradients, you see the rollouts, you can inspect where the model is getting rewarded for the wrong reasons, and you iterate. That tight loop is where a lot of the real learning happens, both for the model and for you as the person designing the task.

With closed models, you mostly don't get to touch the weights, so the environment plays a different role. It becomes an evaluation harness, and increasingly it becomes something you hand to the lab through a fine-tuning API or a partnership. The labs are genuinely hungry for good environments right now because that's the bottleneck. Compute is abundant, the algorithms are mostly understood, but well-specified tasks with reward signals that don't get gamed are scarce. So if you build a really good environment, you have leverage even if you never train a model yourself.

The thing I keep coming back to is that the environment is the thing that transfers. Models get replaced every few months, but a well-designed environment with a robust verifier stays useful across all of them. So I'd encourage people to invest there rather than overfitting to any particular checkpoint. And honestly the hard part isn't the RL, it's writing a reward function that actually captures what you want and holds up when the model starts getting creative about satisfying it.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention distillation or using environment-created examples to train another model.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what do you actually want the model to get better at, and can you build an environment where you can measure that reliably? You need a task, some way for the model to take actions, and feedback that tells you whether those actions accomplished something useful. The hard part is making sure that doing well in the environment corresponds to doing well on the real problem.

With an open model, if you have access to the weights and the training infrastructure, you can close that loop directly: collect rollouts, compute rewards, update the model, and repeat. With a closed model, it depends on what the provider exposes. If you only have an inference API, you can evaluate the model and optimize the system around it, but you’re not directly updating its weights.

In either case, I’d start with a narrow capability and a reward you can really trust. Then I’d check whether improvement transfers to held-out tasks. Otherwise, it’s very easy to build something that gets better at collecting your reward without getting better at the thing you actually care about.

r001.rationale: The response describes using rollouts and rewards to update open models, but says closed models with inference-only APIs can only be evaluated while optimizing the surrounding system. It does not frame RL environments as training-data engines for optimizing both open and closed models.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention distillation or using environment-created examples to train another model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful starting point is: what behavior do you want to improve, and can you build an environment that gives you a trustworthy signal about it? For coding, for example, you can let the model work in a repository, run tests, and see whether it actually solved the problem. That’s much more useful than just asking whether the answer looks good.

Then there’s a separate question of what you can update. With an open model, you can train the weights directly against that feedback. With a closed model, unless the provider exposes a training interface, you’re mostly optimizing the system around it—the prompts, the tools, the way you manage context. You can use the same environment to measure progress, but the optimization happens in different places.

The hard part in either case is making sure success in your environment means something outside it. Models can get very good at exploiting whatever signal you give them. So I’d want varied tasks, held-out evaluations, and checks that the model is learning a useful capability rather than just finding a shortcut to a high reward.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes using RL environments to provide feedback for training open models or optimizing a closed model’s surrounding system, but does not frame those environments as engines for creating training data for either.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention distillation or using environment-created examples to train another model.
